lead: An RC oscillator chooses its frequency by phase, not by resonance. Three RC sections can shift a signal by 180° at one frequency, and an inverting amplifier adds the other 180°. A Wien network does the same with one lead-lag pair at 0° but returns only one third of the output. Both satisfy the Barkhausen condition at a single frequency set by R and C. They are the standard audio sine sources in function generators and the first oscillator built in most analog labs.
prereq: You need 4.4 for the loop conditions, 4.1 for the feedback fraction, and the RC frequency response and inverting amplifier from Units 3 and 2.

sections.h3: Three identical RC sections make 180° at one frequency

blocks.text: An RC phase-shift oscillator uses only resistors and capacitors. Three identical sections are connected as a ladder. Each section has a resistor and a capacitor, and the sections load each other. At very low frequency the capacitors block the signal. At very high frequency the capacitors short it. Somewhere between, the total phase shift through the three sections passes through 180°.

blocks.where: R is the resistance in each section in ohms (Ω); C is the capacitance in each section in farads (F); f₀ is the oscillation frequency in hertz (Hz).

blocks.text: At f₀ the network also attenuates the signal: it returns only 1/29 of the output to the amplifier input. That number comes from the same ladder solution, not from three isolated filters.

The amplifier must therefore have a voltage gain magnitude of at least 29. It must also invert, because the RC network already supplies 180°; the amplifier's 180° makes the total loop phase 360°. A single BJT in common emitter inverts and can give a gain above 29 if its bias and hfe allow it. An op-amp inverting amplifier with Rf/Ri = 29 is the cleaner choice; see Unit 2 for the inverting amplifier.

The circuit is simple and needs no inductor, but it needs high gain and three matched RC sections. Tuning is awkward: changing frequency means changing all three resistors or all three capacitors together. It is used as a fixed-frequency audio source in labs.

sections.h3: The Wien bridge: one lead-lag pair, gain of three

blocks.text: The Wien bridge uses one series RC branch and one parallel RC branch. The series branch is R and C in series from the output to the amplifier input. The parallel branch is R and C in parallel from that input to ground. The two branches form a lead-lag network: one branch leads, the other lags.

blocks.where: β is the fraction of the output fed back; ω = 2πf is angular frequency in rad/s; R and C are the matched resistance in ohms and capacitance in farads.

blocks.text: The phase of β is zero at ωRC = 1. At that point β = 1/3 exactly. So f₀ = 1/(2πRC). The amplifier must be non-inverting with a gain of 3: 1 + Rf/Ri = 3, so Rf = 2Ri. At f₀ the loop phase is 0° from the network plus 0° from the non-inverting amplifier, a total of 0° or 360°.

The Wien bridge needs only one R-C pair to set frequency, has low gain and low distortion, and tunes easily with a ganged variable resistor. It is the standard audio sine oscillator in function generators.

sections.h3: Starting, stabilising and choosing between them

blocks.text: If the loop gain is exactly 1, the oscillator sits on the edge. Any small drift stops it. In practice the gain is set a little above the threshold so oscillation starts from noise and grows. Then a nonlinear element reduces the gain to 1 at the desired amplitude.

A common method uses a small incandescent lamp in the Wien bridge feedback divider. The lamp is Ri, the resistor to ground. Gain is 1 + Rf/R_lamp. When the output amplitude rises, the lamp heats, its resistance rises, and the gain falls. When the output falls, the lamp cools and the gain rises. The amplitude settles where the average gain is 3.
A thermistor works the same way. A diode limiter is cheaper but clips the peaks and adds distortion. The lamp or thermistor is gentler and keeps a clean sine wave.

Use the phase-shift circuit when you need a cheap fixed audio frequency and have gain to spare. Use the Wien bridge when you need a clean, tunable sine wave. Both are RC oscillators; LC and crystal oscillators take over when you need higher Q and better stability, as 4.6 and 4.7 show.

figure.caption: The Wien network returns one third of the output at ωRC = 1 and much less away from it; the flat line is the 1/3 design value.

examples.question: Design an RC phase-shift oscillator for 1 kHz using C = 10 nF in each section. Find R and the minimum amplifier gain. Then use the same R and C in a Wien bridge and find its frequency and required gain.
steps: For the three-section circuit, f₀ = 1/(2πRC√6). Rearrange: R = 1/(2πf₀C√6).
Choose the standard value R = 6.5 kΩ. The actual frequency is then 1/(2π × 6500 × 10⁻⁸ × 2.449) = 999.6 Hz, close enough to 1 kHz.
The RC network gives β = 1/29 at f₀, so the inverting amplifier must have |A| ≥ 29. For an op-amp inverting amplifier, Rf/Ri = 29; pick Ri = 10 kΩ and Rf = 290 kΩ.
Use the same R = 6.5 kΩ and C = 10 nF in a Wien bridge. f = 1/(2πRC) = 1/(2π × 6500 × 10⁻⁸) = 2448.5 Hz ≈ 2449 Hz.
The Wien network gives β = 1/3 at f₀, so the non-inverting amplifier gain is 3: 1 + Rf/Ri = 3, hence Rf = 2Ri. With Ri = 10 kΩ, Rf = 20 kΩ.
examples.answer: R = 6.5 kΩ with an inverting gain of at least 29 for the 1 kHz phase-shift oscillator; the same R and C in a Wien bridge give about 2449 Hz with a non-inverting gain of 3.
examples.check:
import math
C = 10e-9
f_target = 1000.0
R = 6500.0
sqrt6 = math.sqrt(6)
print(R/1000)
print(29.0)
f_wien = 1/(2*math.pi*R*C)
print(int(round(f_wien)))
print(3.0)

traps: Using 1/(2πRC) for the three-section phase-shift oscillator. The √6 belongs there; the Wien bridge has no √6.
Forgetting that the phase-shift amplifier must invert. Without the extra 180°, the loop phase is wrong and the circuit does not oscillate.
Setting the Wien gain to 2 or 4. At f₀ β = 1/3, so the non-inverting gain must be 3: Rf = 2Ri.
Assuming the RC network is unloaded. The 1/29 and the frequency formula come from the loaded ladder; a high-impedance amplifier input and a low-impedance output are needed.
Designing gain exactly 29 or 3 and expecting oscillation to start. Component tolerance and drift mean you start slightly above and use amplitude limiting.

quiz.q: State the Barkhausen condition for oscillation in words and as two equations.
quiz.a: The loop gain must have magnitude 1 and total loop phase 0° or a whole multiple of 360° at the oscillation frequency: |Aβ| = 1 and ∠Aβ = 0° (or 360°).

quiz.q: Why must the amplifier in a three-section RC phase-shift oscillator be inverting?
quiz.a: The three RC sections give 180° of phase shift at f₀. The amplifier must add another 180° so the total loop phase is 360°. A non-inverting amplifier would give 180° total and fail the Barkhausen phase condition.

quiz.q: An RC phase-shift oscillator uses C = 10 nF per section and must run at 2 kHz. Find R and the minimum amplifier gain.
quiz.a: R = 1/(2πf C √6) = 1/(2π × 2000 × 10 × 10⁻⁹ × 2.449) = 1/(3.078 × 10⁻⁴) = 3249 Ω, about 3.25 kΩ. The minimum gain magnitude is 29, and the amplifier must invert.

quiz.q: A Wien bridge oscillator uses R = 3.2 kΩ and C = 10 nF. Find f₀ and the amplifier gain.
quiz.a: f₀ = 1/(2πRC) = 1/(2π × 3200 × 10 × 10⁻⁹) = 4974 Hz, about 5 kHz. The non-inverting gain must be 3, so Rf = 2Ri.

quiz.q: The lamp in a Wien bridge becomes hotter as the output rises. Explain how this holds the amplitude steady.
quiz.a: The lamp is Ri to ground, so gain = 1 + Rf/R_lamp. A rising output heats the lamp, R_lamp rises, and the gain falls toward 3. If the output falls, the lamp cools, R_lamp falls, and the gain rises. This negative feedback on amplitude settles the output at a steady level.

quiz.q: An RC phase-shift oscillator is built with an inverting amplifier of gain 20. The RC network is ideal. Does it oscillate? Give a reason.
quiz.a: No. At f₀ the three-section network returns β = 1/29, so the loop gain magnitude is 20/29, which is less than 1. The Barkhausen magnitude condition is not met, so any oscillation decays.

quiz.q: Give two reasons a Wien bridge is easier to tune than a three-section RC phase-shift oscillator.
quiz.a: The Wien bridge has one frequency-setting R-C pair, so one ganged control can tune it; the phase-shift circuit needs three resistors or three capacitors to change together. The Wien bridge also needs a gain of only 3, not 29, which makes the amplifier design easier.

beyond: Not for the exam. In the lab, the Wien bridge is the analog heart of many audio signal generators, and a lamp-stabilised version is a standard construction project. Modern instruments often generate sine waves digitally (direct digital synthesis) and use the analog oscillator only as a backup or for low-distortion audio. Search for 'Wien bridge lamp stabilisation', 'RC phase-shift oscillator loading', and 'function generator DDS vs analog' to go further.
